title: AdaStep: Adaptive Step Credit Weighting for Agentic Reinforcement Learning

paper.title: AdaStep: Adaptive Step Credit Weighting for Agentic Reinforcement Learning
paper.abstract:
Abstract Long-horizon LLM agents are typically trained with sparse outcome rewards, making trajectory-level objectives too coarse to distinguish the contribution of individual decisions.
Step-level credit assignment provides finer-grained supervision, but its estimates can be unreliable because observed returns also depend on subsequent actions, environment transitions, and trajectory length.
We propose AdaStep , an Ada ptive Step -credit weighting method that controls how strongly each group-derived local advantage modifies the trajectory-level signal.
We formulate this weighting as a mean-squared-error estimation problem for the latent step advantage and, under an explicit conditional sampling assumption, derive an optimal per-state shrinkage coefficient.
The coefficient admits a signal-to-total-variance interpretation: it preserves local credit when return variation is attributable to the selected action and suppresses it when variation is dominated by downstream randomness.
AdaStep requires only lightweight scalar computation, with no critic, additional rollouts, or extra model inference.
Experiments with three model backbones on ALFWorld, WebShop, and ScienceWorld show consistent improvements over baselines at low computational cost.

sections.heading: 1 Introduction
sections.text: Figure 1: The episode-level advantage provides an accurate but coarse signal of trajectory outcomes, while the step-level advantage offers finer-grained but noisy local credit. In GiGPO, combining these signals with equal weights can assign negative advantages to useful actions or excessively large positive advantages to actions unrelated to success. AdaStep retains the episode-level signal and adaptively weights the local correction for each step-level group. Large language models (LLMs) are increasingly moving from chat-based interaction to agentic decision making ( Yao et al., 2023 ; Zhou et al., 2024 ; Wang et al., 2026 ; Zheng et al., 2026 ) . Unlike a chat model, which primarily maps a prompt to a response, an agent repeatedly interacts with an external environment by observing states, taking actions, and receiving subsequent states and rewards. Completing a task therefore requires coordinating a sequence of decisions whose consequences may unfold over a long horizon. Meanwhile, group-based reinforcement learning has become an important paradigm for LLM post-training ( Yu et al., 2025 ; Min et al., 2026 ; Zhang et al., 2026 ; Liu et al., 2026 ) , offering a simple, critic-free learning signal. Given multiple rollouts of the same task, the mean return serves as an empirical estimate of the task-level value, and each rollout’s return relative to this mean provides an advantage estimate, without requiring a separately trained critic ( Shao et al., 2024 ; Yu et al., 2025 ) . Under binary success rewards, successful trajectories receive nonnegative advantages and failed trajectories receive nonpositive advantages. Sparse, delayed rewards make it difficult to identify which intermediate actions contributed to an eventual outcome ( Arjona-Medina et al., 2019 ) . For agentic tasks, however, the long-horizon nature of decision making exposes a fundamental limitation of trajectory-level credit assignment in Group Relative Policy Optimization (GRPO) ( Shao et al., 2024 ) . By broadcasting the same outcome-based advantage to every state–action pair along a trajectory, GRPO provides a global but coarse learning signal: it does not distinguish actions that contributed to success from those that were irrelevant or erroneous, nor does it identify which decisions were responsible for failure. Consequently, useful actions in failed trajectories may be penalized, while unhelpful actions in successful trajectories may be reinforced. To address this coarse credit assignment, Group in GRPO (GiGPO) ( Feng et al., 2025 ) augments the trajectory-level advantage with a local, step-level correction. It groups state–action pairs sharing the same anchor state across rollouts and uses the group’s mean discounted return as an empirical state-value baseline. Each sampled return is then compared with this baseline to obtain a step-level relative advantage. This construction provides finer-grained credit assignment while preserving critic-free estimation. However, these local advantages are estimated from finite samples, and their credibility can vary across step-level groups ( Li et al., 2026 ) . Step-level credit provides finer supervision, but its estimates are affected by downstream randomness. Even for the same state–action pair, stochastic transitions, subsequent actions, and discounted reward timing can produce advantage estimates with opposite signs. Strong local corrections may therefore amplify estimation noise, whereas weak corrections may suppress useful action information. This trade-off connects to variance control in advantage estimation ( Schulman et al., 2015 ) and shrinkage-based reward-baseline estimation with limited rollouts ( Zeng et al., 2026 ) . GiGPO ( Feng et al., 2025 ) adds a local step-level correction to the global trajectory-level advantage using a fixed coefficient. However, this correction can differ in credibility across anchor-state groups. In some groups, return differences mainly reflect differences in action quality, making the local estimates useful for guiding policy updates. In others, much of the return variation arises from subsequent decisions or stochastic transitions, even when the same action is taken. Such variation makes the local estimates less credible. A fixed coefficient cannot adapt to these differences: a large weight may amplify noisy corrections, while a small weight may weaken useful local signals. We propose AdaStep , which retains the global advantage as a reference and adapts the local step-level correction strength to each group’s estimation credibility, as illustrated in Figure 1 . We derive the coefficient under a mean-squared-error objective and estimate it from existing rollout statistics, requiring no critic, additional rollouts, or extra model forward passes. Our main contributions are as follows: 1. An estimation formulation of local credit assignment. Taking the trajectory-level advantage as a reference, we formulate local advantage weighting as an estimation problem for the true step-level advantage. This formulation makes explicit the trade-off between preserving useful local signals and suppressing sampling error. 2. A principled correction coefficient for each group. Under the proposed objective and stated assumptions, we derive the optimal correction coefficient and obtain a computationally tractable expression that adapts the strength of local correction to the estimation credibility of each step-level group. 3. Empirical gains across three benchmarks. Experiments on three agent-task benchmarks demonstrate that the proposed correction improves performance, supporting the value of accounting for local estimation credibility in group-relative credit assignment. AdaStep tops all trained baselines, gaining up to +9.36 points over GiGPO. 4. Minimal computational overhead. The method requires only a lightweight coefficient computation for each step-level group and integrates directly into the existing advantage calculation with minimal additional time and memory costs, adding about 1% credit-computation time.

sections.heading: 2 Related Work
sections.text: Reinforcement learning for large language models. Beyond preference alignment through RLHF, reinforcement learning is increasingly used to enhance LLM reasoning and decision making. Group-based methods, including RLOO ( Ahmadian et al., 2024 ) , GRPO ( Shao et al., 2024 ) , Dr. GRPO ( Liu et al., 2025 ) , DAPO ( Yu et al., 2025 ) , and CPPO ( Lin et al., 2025 ) , provide scalable alternatives to PPO ( Schulman et al., 2017 ) . These methods estimate relative advantages from multiple responses to the same prompt, eliminating the need for a separately trained value function and reducing training costs. Recent work further advances this framework through hybrid token–sequence optimization in DHPO ( Min et al., 2026 ) , adaptive rollout selection in AERO ( Zhang et al., 2026 ) , and length-unbiased sequence-level optimization in LUSPO ( Liu et al., 2026 ) , emphasizing efficiency, robustness, and bias reduction in LLM post-training. Step-level advantage assignment. GiGPO estimates step-level advantages by grouping state–action pairs with shared anchor states across rollouts. HGPO ( He et al., 2026 ) and ProGPO ( Fan and Liu, 2026 ) extend this idea through additional grouping mechanisms, introducing further computational costs. Critic-based approaches such as CAPO ( Xie et al., 2025 ) and SAPO ( Liang et al., 2026 ) incur the time and memory costs of training a critic, while EnvRL ( Wang et al., 2026 ) adds auxiliary supervision through state prediction and inverse dynamics. PGPO ( Zheng et al., 2026 ) refines step-level advantage signals but does not explicitly address how to control their correction strength. ECPO ( Li et al., 2026 ) constructs heuristically motivated calibrated action-level advantages, whereas AdaStep retains the occurrence-level estimator and derives its state-specific scaling from an explicit estimation objective. Our analysis accounts for the action-conditional bias induced by the shared group baseline, while exploiting the cancellation of this bias after marginalizing over actions.

sections.text: We consider a general setting in which an LLM agent interacts with an environment to complete multi-step tasks described by a task prompt x ∼ p ⁡ ( X ) x\sim p(X) . At each discrete time step t = 1 , 2 , … , T t=1,2,\dots,T , the environment is in a state s t ∈ 𝒮 s_{t}\in\mathcal{S} and the agent generates a textual action a t ∈ 𝒜 t a_{t}\in\mathcal{A}_{t} , where in this text world the action space is 𝒜 t = 𝒱 n \mathcal{A}_{t}=\mathcal{V}^{n} , with 𝒱 \mathcal{V} the token vocabulary and n n the maximum generation length. In text worlds, 𝒮 \mathcal{S} is typically a finite discrete set whose elements consist of text. After executing a t a_{t} , the environment returns a scalar reward r t ∈ ℝ r_{t}\in\mathbb{R} and transitions to the next state s t + 1 s_{t+1} according to P P . A full episode consists of a trajectory τ = { ( s 1 , a 1 , r 1 ) , ( s 2 , a 2 , r 2 ) , … , ( s T , a T , r T ) } \tau=\big\{(s_{1},a_{1},r_{1}),(s_{2},a_{2},r_{2}),\dots,(s_{T},a_{T},r_{T})\big\} with horizon T T . In many realistic scenarios the environment provides sparse or delayed rewards (e.g., success and failure signals at the end of an episode). Because the agent generates T T consecutive textual actions ( a 1 , … , a T ) (a_{1},\dots,a_{T}) , each potentially spanning thousands of tokens, assigning credit to individual tokens over the course of an episode is particularly challenging. sections.heading: 4.1 Motivation
sections.text: In policy-gradient methods, for a state-action pair with positive advantage, the gradient update increases its probability under the new policy relative to the old policy, and decreases it for pairs with negative advantage. The problem is that GRPO’s global trajectory-level signal is too coarse: it reflects only whether the entire trajectory succeeds and carries no information about which decisions caused the task to succeed or fail. GiGPO’s results show that adding a local advantage correction to the global advantage does improve performance. However, step-level advantages are based on the state-action return of the current trajectory, which is affected by randomness in the subsequent trajectory and therefore cannot always faithfully reflect the true advantage of a state-action pair. Example 1 . A task requires purchasing meat snacks with the three meat flavor and the 3 pack option. At the same product-detail-page state, two trajectories both execute click[three meat] , correctly selecting the requested flavor. The shorter trajectory then selects the pack size and completes the purchase in 8 steps. The longer trajectory also selects the correct pack size but returns to the search results and browses additional pages before succeeding in 23 steps. Due to return discounting and within-group comparisons, GiGPO assigns advantages of 3.33 3.33 and − 1.51 -1.51 to this same correct action in the shorter and longer trajectories, respectively. This negative advantage is misleading: the action is correct in both cases, and the difference arises from stochastic subsequent behavior rather than from the action itself. Our method assigns advantages of 1.07 1.07 and 0.35 0.35 , respectively, correcting the sign in the longer trajectory and reducing the discrepancy between the advantages assigned to the same state–action pair. Example 2 . A task requires placing a cooled pot on a stove. At the state described by “You arrive at sinkbasin 1. On the sinkbasin 1, you see a apple 1, a egg 1, and a lettuce 1”, multiple trajectories execute clean pot 1 with sinkbasin 1 . However, cleaning the pot does not cool it. Within one group, this action occurs four times. One trajectory succeeds through subsequent correct actions and receives a positive return, whereas the other three have zero return. GiGPO assigns the cleaning action an advantage of 4.13 4.13 in the successful trajectory and − 0.74 -0.74 in each of the other three. This positive credit is misleading because the cleaning action itself does not satisfy the cooling requirement; success results from later actions. Our method changes these advantages to 0.86 0.86 and − 0.56 -0.56 , respectively. The local step-level signal is therefore valuable but not fully credible, and how strongly to trust it (i.e., how to control the strength of the step-level correction) is an important question. sections.heading: 5 Experiments
sections.text: We evaluate AdaStep using three backbone models, Qwen3-1.7B, Qwen3-4B, and Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct, on three benchmarks: ALFWorld, WebShop, and ScienceWorld. We compare against closed-source model baselines, prompting methods such as ReAct, and reinforcement learning algorithms including GRPO, GiGPO, and HGPO. Detailed benchmark descriptions, baselines, and implementation settings are provided in Appendix C .

sections.heading: 5.1 Main results
sections.text: Table 1 compares AdaStep with prompting-based and RL baselines across three models and three benchmarks. AdaStep consistently outperforms HGPO and GiGPO across all model–benchmark combinations, with more pronounced gains over GRPO and PPO. These results support the effectiveness of reliability-aware step-level credit assignment across different model scales and task environments.

sections.text: In practice, some step-level groups contain only one distinct action, only one return observation per action, or identical returns, as illustrated in Table 3 (a). We therefore estimate the coefficient in Theorem 2 only for groups containing at least two distinct actions, at least two return observations per action, and positive total return variance. Groups with identical returns have zero step-level advantages and require no correction. For other groups that do not meet the estimation criteria, we compare three default weights: w = 0 w=0 , w = w ¯ w=\bar{w} , and w = 1 w=1 , where w ¯ \bar{w} is the mean coefficient over eligible groups in the current batch when such groups exist. Eligible groups use their estimated coefficients in all three variants. On WebShop and ALFWorld with Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct, w = 1 w=1 achieves the highest observed success rate among the three choices (Table 3 (b)), supporting retention of the original step-level signal when evidence is insufficient for coefficient estimation. sections.heading: 5.5 Analysis of step-credit estimation on WebShop
sections.text: We examine step-credit estimation on 3,666 historical WebShop anchor-state groups using two complementary diagnostics. Within-action variation measures the remaining fluctuation among weighted credits assigned to the same action. Held-out reference MSE measures their squared deviation from action-level advantages estimated using a separate subset of samples. Appendix E describes the coefficient estimation, sample splitting, and metric definitions. Figure 3 (c,d) shows that AdaStep reduces within-action variation while achieving the lowest held-out reference MSE. This suggests a better balance between suppressing fluctuations and preserving action-level information, as reducing variation alone does not guarantee better estimation.

sections.heading: 6 Conclusion
sections.text: We introduced AdaStep, which derives an optimal per-state shrinkage coefficient from a mean-squared-error objective on the latent step advantage and reads it as the fraction of return variance explained by the selected action. Across three backbones and three benchmarks, AdaStep consistently improves over GRPO, GiGPO, and HGPO, with gains that persist with and without advantage normalization, at negligible computational cost. Extending AdaStep to continuous or partially observable environments, where anchor states cannot be matched directly, remains open and is discussed in Appendix F .

sections.heading: Appendix B Pseudo Code
sections.text: Algorithm 1 summarizes the AdaStep training procedure, following the rollout, grouping, and policy-update structure of GiGPO ( Feng et al., 2025 ) . AdaStep replaces the fixed coefficient ω \omega with a coefficient estimated separately for each anchor-state group; the corresponding operations are italicized in the algorithm. Within each task, we use anchor states as hash-table keys to collect step-level groups, and further partition each group by the observed action to estimate within-action return variability. These statistics can be accumulated using counts, sums, and sums of squared returns, without an additional critic or additional rollouts.

sections.heading: Appendix C Experimental Details
sections.text: Benchmarks. We evaluate on three long-horizon benchmarks: ALFWorld ( Shridhar et al., 2021 ) , WebShop ( Yao et al., 2022 ) , and ScienceWorld ( Wang et al., 2022 ) . ALFWorld is a text-based embodied environment in which agents complete multi-step household tasks, such as heating, cleaning, and relocating objects, with sparse rewards upon task completion; we set the maximum number of environment steps to 50. WebShop is a simulated shopping environment with 1.18 million products, requiring agents to search, select product options, and purchase items that satisfy natural-language instructions; we set the maximum number of environment steps to 30. ScienceWorld is a text-based scientific reasoning environment in which agents conduct virtual experiments such as measuring melting points and testing electrical conductivity; we set the maximum number of environment steps to 30. In our experiments, ScienceWorld evaluation is restricted to eight simple tasks. Baselines. We compare against baselines across three categories: (1) Frontier models: DeepSeek-V4.1-Flash ( DeepSeek-AI et al., 2026 ) and GLM-5.2 ( GLM-5-Team et al., 2026 ) , evaluated with ReAct prompting ( Yao et al., 2023 ) as reference points for frontier model capabilities. (2) Prompting methods: ReAct ( Yao et al., 2023 ) , which interleaves reasoning and actions, and Reflexion ( Shinn et al., 2023 ) , which uses verbal self-reflection and episodic memory to improve subsequent attempts without updating model parameters. (3) RL training methods: PPO ( Schulman et al., 2017 ) , a standard actor–critic algorithm; GRPO ( Shao et al., 2024 ) and GiGPO ( Feng et al., 2025 ) , which estimate relative advantages from trajectory groups without learned critics, with GiGPO additionally using step-level groups for fine-grained credit assignment; and HGPO ( He et al., 2026 ) , which incorporates historical context into anchor-state grouping and adaptively aggregates advantages across hierarchical groups to reduce bias in step-level advantage estimation. Implementation. We use Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct ( Qwen et al., 2025 ) , Qwen3-4B, and Qwen3-1.7B ( Yang et al., 2025 ) as backbone models. All Qwen3 models are run with their built-in thinking mode disabled throughout training and evaluation. For fair comparison, all RL methods share the same training pipeline and common hyperparameters specified below. We follow the hyperparameter configuration of GiGPO ( Feng et al., 2025 ) for ALFWorld and WebShop, with the WebShop episode limit extended from 15 to 30 steps. sections.heading: Appendix F Limitations and Future Work
sections.text: AdaStep estimates its adaptive coefficient from the return statistics of the samples that share an anchor state, so it relies on constructing step-level state groups across multiple rollouts. In the three benchmarks studied here, the environment state is discrete and exactly reproduced, so identical states can be matched directly and the groups required for estimation are readily available. In more general settings, such as continuous, partially observable, or open-ended environments, the same situation is rarely revisited verbatim, and how to define and construct state groups that remain suitable for the variance-ratio estimate is an open question. We therefore leave the design of state abstractions or learned grouping criteria that preserve the reliability interpretation of w ∗ ​ ( 𝒔 ) w^{*}(\bm{s}) to future work.

Affiliation: Tsinghua University Nanjing University Affiliation: Xiaomi Inc. † zhiwang@nju.edu.cn , {shaokun,luanjian}@xiaomi.com Abstract Long-horizon LLM agents are typically trained with sparse outcome rewards, making trajectory-level objectives too coarse to distinguish the contribution of individual decisions. Step-level credit assignment provides finer-grained supervision, but its estimates can be unreliable because observed returns also depend on subsequent actions, environment transitions, and trajectory length. We propose AdaStep , an Ada ptive Step -credit weighting method that controls how strongly each group-derived local advantage modifies the trajectory-level signal. We formulate this weighting as a mean-squared-error estimation problem for the latent step advantage and, under an explicit conditional sampling assumption, derive an optimal per-state shrinkage coefficient. The coefficient admits a signal-to-total-variance interpretation: it preserves local credit when return variation is attributable to the selected action and suppresses it when variation is dominated by downstream randomness. AdaStep requires only lightweight scalar computation, with no critic, additional rollouts, or extra model inference. Experiments with three model backbones on ALFWorld, WebShop, and ScienceWorld show consistent improvements over baselines at low computational cost. 1 Introduction Figure 1: The episode-level advantage provides an accurate but coarse signal of trajectory outcomes, while the step-level advantage offers finer-grained but noisy local credit. In GiGPO, combining these signals with equal weights can assign negative advantages to useful actions or excessively large positive advantages to actions unrelated to success. AdaStep retains the episode-level signal and adaptively weights the local correction for each step-level group. Large language models (LLMs) are increasingly moving from chat-based interaction to agentic decision making ( Yao et al., 2023 ; Zhou et al., 2024 ; Wang et al., 2026 ; Zheng et al., 2026 ) . Unlike a chat model, which primarily maps a prompt to a response, an agent repeatedly interacts with an external environment by observing states, taking actions, and receiving subsequent states and rewards. Completing a task therefore requires coordinating a sequence of decisions whose consequences may unfold over a long horizon. Meanwhile, group-based reinforcement learning has become an important paradigm for LLM post-training ( Yu et al., 2025 ; Min et al., 2026 ; Zhang et al., 2026 ; Liu et al., 2026 ) , offering a simple, critic-free learning signal. Given multiple rollouts of the same task, the mean return serves as an empirical estimate of the task-level value, and each rollout’s return relative to this mean provides an advantage estimate, without requiring a separately trained critic ( Shao et al., 2024 ; Yu et al., 2025 ) . Under binary success rewards, successful trajectories receive nonnegative advantages and failed trajectories receive nonpositive advantages. Sparse, delayed rewards make it difficult to identify which intermediate actions contributed to an eventual outcome ( Arjona-Medina et al., 2019 ) . For agentic tasks, however, the long-horizon nature of decision making exposes a fundamental limitation of trajectory-level credit assignment in Group Relative Policy Optimization (GRPO) ( Shao et al., 2024 ) . By broadcasting the same outcome-based advantage to every state–action pair along a trajectory, GRPO provides a global but coarse learning signal: it does not distinguish actions that contributed to success from those that were irrelevant or erroneous, nor does it identify which decisions were responsible for failure. Consequently, useful actions in failed trajectories may be penalized, while unhelpful actions in successful trajectories may be reinforced. To address this coarse credit assignment, Group in GRPO (GiGPO) ( Feng et al., 2025 ) augments the trajectory-level advantage with a local, step-level correction. It groups state–action pairs sharing the same anchor state across rollouts and uses the group’s mean discounted return as an empirical state-value baseline. Each sampled return is then compared with this baseline to obtain a step-level relative advantage. This construction provides finer-grained credit assignment while preserving critic-free estimation. However, these local advantages are estimated from finite samples, and their credibility can vary across step-level groups ( Li et al., 2026 ) . Step-level credit provides finer supervision, but its estimates are affected by downstream randomness. Even for the same state–action pair, stochastic transitions, subsequent actions, and discounted reward timing can produce advantage estimates with opposite signs. Strong local corrections may therefore amplify estimation noise, whereas weak corrections may suppress useful action information. This trade-off connects to variance control in advantage estimation ( Schulman et al., 2015 ) and shrinkage-based reward-baseline estimation with limited rollouts ( Zeng et al., 2026 ) . GiGPO ( Feng et al., 2025 ) adds a local step-level correction to the global trajectory-level advantage using a fixed coefficient. However, this correction can differ in credibility across anchor-state groups. In some groups, return differences mainly reflect differences in action quality, making the local estimates useful for guiding policy updates. In others, much of the return variation arises from subsequent decisions or stochastic transitions, even when the same action is taken. Such variation makes the local estimates less credible. A fixed coefficient cannot adapt to these differences: a large weight may amplify noisy corrections, while a small weight may weaken useful local signals. We propose AdaStep , which retains the global advantage as a reference and adapts the local step-level correction strength to each group’s estimation credibility, as illustrated in Figure 1 . We derive the coefficient under a mean-squared-error objective and estimate it from existing rollout statistics, requiring no critic, additional rollouts, or extra model forward passes. Our main contributions are as follows: 1. An estimation formulation of local credit assignment. Taking the trajectory-level advantage as a reference, we formulate local advantage weighting as an estimation problem for the true step-level advantage. This formulation makes explicit the trade-off between preserving useful local signals and suppressing sampling error. 2. A principled correction coefficient for each group. Under the proposed objective and stated assumptions, we derive the optimal correction coefficient and obtain a computationally tractable expression that adapts the strength of local correction to the estimation credibility of each step-level group. 3. Empirical gains across three benchmarks. Experiments on three agent-task benchmarks demonstrate that the proposed correction improves performance, supporting the value of accounting for local estimation credibility in group-relative credit assignment. AdaStep tops all trained baselines, gaining up to +9.36 points over GiGPO. 4. Minimal computational overhead. The method requires only a lightweight coefficient computation for each step-level group and integrates directly into the existing advantage calculation with minimal additional time and memory costs, adding about 1% credit-computation time. 2 Related Work Reinforcement learning for large language models. Beyond preference alignment through RLHF, reinforcement learning is increasingly used to enhance LLM reasoning and decision making. Group-based methods, including RLOO ( Ahmadian et al., 2024 ) , GRPO ( Shao et al., 2024 ) , Dr. GRPO ( Liu et al., 2025 ) , DAPO ( Yu et al., 2025 ) , and CPPO ( Lin et al., 2025 ) , provide scalable alternatives to PPO ( Schulman et al., 2017 ) . These methods estimate relative advantages from multiple responses to the same prompt, eliminating the need for a separately trained value function and reducing training costs. Recent work further advances this framework through hybrid token–sequence optimization in DHPO ( Min et al., 2026 ) , adaptive rollout selection in AERO ( Zhang et al., 2026 ) , and length-unbiased sequence-level optimization in LUSPO ( Liu et al., 2026 ) , emphasizing efficiency, robustness, and bias reduction in LLM post-training. Step-level advantage assignment. GiGPO estimates step-level advantages by grouping state–action pairs with shared anchor states across rollouts. HGPO ( He et al., 2026 ) and ProGPO ( Fan and Liu, 2026 ) extend this idea through additional grouping mechanisms, introducing further computational costs. Critic-based approaches such as CAPO ( Xie et al., 2025 ) and SAPO ( Liang et al., 2026 ) incur the time and memory costs of training a critic, while EnvRL ( Wang et al., 2026 ) adds auxiliary supervision through state prediction and inverse dynamics. PGPO ( Zheng et al., 2026 ) refines step-level advantage signals but does not explicitly address how to control their correction strength. ECPO ( Li et al., 2026 ) constructs heuristically motivated calibrated action-level advantages, whereas AdaStep retains the occurrence-level estimator and derives its state-specific scaling from an explicit estimation objective. Our analysis accounts for the action-conditional bias induced by the shared group baseline, while exploiting the cancellation of this bias after marginalizing over actions. 3 Preliminaries 3.1 Problem setup We consider a general setting in which an LLM agent interacts with an environment to complete multi-step tasks described by a task prompt x ∼ p ⁡ ( X ) x\sim p(X) . We model the environment as a Markov decision process (MDP) ℳ = ( 𝒮 , 𝒜 , P , r , γ ) \mathcal{M}=(\mathcal{S},\mathcal{A},P,r,\gamma) , where 𝒮 \mathcal{S} is the state space of the environment, 𝒜 \mathcal{A} is the action space, P ⁡ ( s t + 1 ∣ s t , a t ) P(s_{t+1}\mid s_{t},a_{t}) is the state transition model, r r is the reward function, and γ \gamma is the discount factor. In text worlds, 𝒮 \mathcal{S} is typically a finite discrete set whose elements consist of text. After executing a t a_{t} , the environment returns a scalar reward r t ∈ ℝ r_{t}\in\mathbb{R} and transitions to the next state s t + 1 s_{t+1} according to P P . A full episode consists of a trajectory τ = { ( s 1 , a 1 , r 1 ) , ( s 2 , a 2 , r 2 ) , … , ( s T , a T , r T ) } \tau=\big\{(s_{1},a_{1},r_{1}),(s_{2},a_{2},r_{2}),\dots,(s_{T},a_{T},r_{T})\big\} with horizon T T . The problem is that GRPO’s global trajectory-level signal is too coarse: it reflects only whether the entire trajectory succeeds and carries no information about which decisions caused the task to succeed or fail. GiGPO’s results show that adding a local advantage correction to the global advantage does improve performance. However, step-level advantages are based on the state-action return of the current trajectory, which is affected by randomness in the subsequent trajectory and therefore cannot always faithfully reflect the true advantage of a state-action pair. Example 1 . A task requires purchasing meat snacks with the three meat flavor and the 3 pack option. At the same product-detail-page state, two trajectories both execute click[three meat] , correctly selecting the requested flavor. The shorter trajectory then selects the pack size and completes the purchase in 8 steps. The longer trajectory also selects the correct pack size but returns to the search results and browses additional pages before succeeding in 23 steps. Due to return discounting and within-group comparisons, GiGPO assigns advantages of 3.33 3.33 and − 1.51 -1.51 to this same correct action in the shorter and longer trajectories, respectively. This negative advantage is misleading: the action is correct in both cases, and the difference arises from stochastic subsequent behavior rather than from the action itself. Our method assigns advantages of 1.07 1.07 and 0.35 0.35 , respectively, correcting the sign in the longer trajectory and reducing the discrepancy between the advantages assigned to the same state–action pair. Example 2 . A task requires placing a cooled pot on a stove. At the state described by “You arrive at sinkbasin 1. On the sinkbasin 1, you see a apple 1, a egg 1, and a lettuce 1”, multiple trajectories execute clean pot 1 with sinkbasin 1 . However, cleaning the pot does not cool it. Within one group, this action occurs four times. One trajectory succeeds through subsequent correct actions and receives a positive return, whereas the other three have zero return. GiGPO assigns the cleaning action an advantage of 4.13 4.13 in the successful trajectory and − 0.74 -0.74 in each of the other three. This positive credit is misleading because the cleaning action itself does not satisfy the cooling requirement; success results from later actions. Our method changes these advantages to 0.86 0.86 and − 0.56 -0.56 , respectively.
